To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there are important differences in the cost-effectiness of managing hypertension in men and women; the differences are due to different costs of managing hypertension in women; and the differences can be eliminated by increasing the cost-effectiveness in the management of women's hypertension.

the cost-effectiveness estimates of Weinstein and Stanson are generally valid for males but not females; that there is substantial variability in the cost of treating hypertension; that there are many potential cost reductions; that the most important cost reduction is in the number of physician visits; and that the most important factor in the number of visits is the number of medications prescribed.

the cost-effectiveness estimates for hypertension management are sensitive to the assumptions made in the analysis and to the characteristics of the population studied, that the cost-effectiness of hypertension management can be increased by as much as 33% by making relatively minor changes in the way hypertension is currently managed by Family Practitioners, and that the cost-effectivenes of hypertension management is not likely to be increased significantly by increasing the frequency of physician office visits or by using more expensive drugs.

the application of cost-effectiveness analysis to the management of hypertension, and the use of this approach to improve the quality of medical care.
a methodological and empirical analysis of the management of hypertension in the context of community care.
the development, application, and evaluation of a new approach to the analysis and control of variability in cost-effectiveness.

the management of hypertension in this Family Practice center appears to be cost-effective, but that there is substantial variability in cost-effectiveness and that this variability can be reduced by modifying current management procedures.
the cost-effectiveness estimates of Weinstein and Stanson for hypertension appear to be valid for males and for women under 45, but not for older women.
the management of hypertension by a Family Practice physician is more cost-effective than previously thought.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cost-effectiveness estimates of Weinstein and Stanson are probably reasonable for the management of hypertension, but that there is a substantial potential for improving cost-effectiveness in many cases.

the cost-effectiveness estimates of Weinstein and Stanson for managing hypertension are reasonable and that the cost-effectives of managing hypertension in a family practice center is similar to that in a general practice center.

there is considerable variability in the cost and effectiveness of treating hypertensives in a community family practice center, but that this variability is not random, and that the cost and effectiveness can be improved in many cases.

there is substantial room for cost-effective improvement of hypertension management in community family practice centers, and that such improvements are possible without major changes in current procedures.
